title.narrative: CO-SGBV Response and Mitigation in Somal

description.narrative:
Prolonged and recurring conflict across the Horn of Africa and the Sahel has resulted in dire humanitarian needs and forced millions of people to flee their homes, adopt negative coping mechanisms, and increased exposure to a multitude of risks. The disputed regions of Sool and Sanaag face ongoing cyclical humanitarian crises, armed conflict, drought and flooding. It is estimated up to 203,000 people are living in IDP settlements in Las Anood district or neighbouring districts including Buhoodle in Togdheer. Despite fighting ending, the situation remains very tense with high humanitarian needs among both displaced and host communities. Protection monitoring mechanisms found an upward trend of SGBV, particularly IPV and assault.[6] Oxfam’s 2023 GPA found that rape was the biggestprotection concern reported by women (59%) and girls (55.4%). Conflict has compounded the impacts of a drought ongoing since 2017 and 43% of people (214,000) in Sool and Togdheer regions are in IPC 3 ‘Crisis’ (including most IDP settlements) and IPC 4 ’Emergency’(including IDP and urban populations of Las Anood). Oxfam’s 2023 IRNA found widespread household income vulnerability, with 60% of HH experiencing declining income, 58% of HHs spending more than half of their income onfood and 18% on water.
Oxfam’s work is guided by its Gender in Emergencies Strategy (2022–2025) and Gender Standards (2022) and grounded in feminist theory and practice. These frame an effective, holistic and comprehensive approach to humanitarian action that acknowledges and addresses gender in a responsive, appropriate, and equitable manner. Oxfam’s global experience and expertise leading SGBV, SRH and GiE programming makes it well placed to respond to the increased risk of SGBV in humanitarian contexts and deliver life-saving SRH information and services. Oxfam staff and partners mainstream gender through its WASH and Protection work, as well as gender-targeted action, which includes SRH, SGBV risk mitigation, prevention and response and women’s leadership. Oxfam has a large global portfolio of programming, including ongoing programming in the proposed target communities that aims to address gender inequality and the gendered impacts of humanitarian crises.
Oxfam, together with six local implementing partners, propose to implement a multi-country, multi-sectorial, survivor-centred approach to respond to the intersectional SRH, SGBV and protection needs identified by SGBV survivors, while also mitigating SGBV exposure through community-based protection mechanisms, rehabilitation and provision of critical WASH infrastructure and hygiene items.
Oxfam will work with partners, APLFT, We-Action, Mums for Mums, KAALO, ATAD and UNIJED who have extensive experience implementing humanitarian programming, including SGBV and protection work. The program will contribute towards reduced suffering, increased protection and lives saved of women, men, boys and girls, especially SGBV survivors, in targeted conflict and crisis-affected communities in South Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso and Chad over 24 months. The proposed intervention is aligned with the CERF Lifesaving Criteria, Inter-Agency Minimum Standards for Gender-Based Violence in Emergencies Programming, Inter-Agency Field Manual on Reproductive Health in Humanitarian Settings, WHO’s Clinical Management of Rape and Intimate Partner Violence Survivors: Developing Protocols for Use in Humanitarian Settings, IASC Guidelines for Integrating Gender-based Violence Interventions in Humanitarian Action and the Humanitarian Response Plans (HRP) in all five countries.
The target communities are IPC level 3, 4 and 5, in areas with high reported levels of SGBV, recurring or recently ended conflict, and facing multiple other crises including drought and near-famine like conditions. Oxfam and partners will prioritize communities with large displaced populations and limited access to infrastructure and resources to meet their basic needs. Across the targeted communities, Oxfam plans to reach approximately 242,962 individuals, including 88,592 women, 59,503 men, 52,092 girls and 42,775 boys, 10% of whom will be people living with disabilities (PLWDs). Anestimated 70% of people assisted will come from out-of-camp IDP populations and the remaining 30% fromthe host community. The Ultimate Outcome of the program is reduced suffering, increased protection and lives saved of women, men, boys and girls, especially SGBVsurvivors, in conflict-affected target communities in South Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Burkina Faso and Chad. Oxfam will achieve this goal by responding to identified SRH and SGBV needs, while mitigating SGBV exposure through strengthening community-based protection mechanisms, and rehabilitation of critical WASH infrastructure and hygiene items.
The transition, exit and sustainability of gains has been considered throughout the design of this program. Community members, community leaders and local and technical authorities will be supported by Oxfam and partners to draw up exit plans at theoutset. These will include a reflection on the achievements of the program and identification of key activities to be carried out beyond the program life. The exit strategy in each context willbe based on several integrated mechanisms.

participating-org.narrative: In 2004 Oxfam Novib set up a Liaison Office in Nairobi, Kenya in order to support the Strengthening Somali Civil Society Program, at the request of the EU. This request was based on Oxfam Novib's work in Somalia to date, but intended to be more widely directed atthe entire civil society sector and the specific context in which it is operating in a post-conflict country. The program started with consulting local organisations in Somalia and Somaliland to get a complete picture of the sectors and regions where they are active, the challenges they face and the relationship between civil society, local political structures and the private sector. A program was then developed to strengthen the institutional development of Oxfam Novib's partners and those of other Oxfams, as well as a range of new NGOs. In the first year local consultants were trained in Somalia. They were then seconded to civil society organisations to build their capacity in financial and organisational management. Furthermore, workshops were organised on specific themes suchas human rights and the role of civil society in the Somali context. The Liaison Office is now going to support the expansion of the program, focussing on strengthening both organisation and project management, while facilitating more training in the fields of civic education, governance, human rights and women's rights, HIV and AIDS and child protection. Over the years, the Somalia Country Office has expanded its intervention on short term humanitarian response as well as development development interventions. In 2015/2016, a decision was reached to move the Country Programme operation, which was largely in Nairobi, from Nairobi to Hargeisa. The country office has a small office in Nairobi , Kenya and large operations office in Hargeisa, Somaliland.
